title: Friction
subject: Physics

English.simple_explanation: Friction is a force that resists sliding between two surfaces that are touching.
English.detailed_explanation: Where two surfaces touch, tiny irregularities and attractions between them resist sliding. Friction always acts opposite to the motion, or opposite to the direction something is being pushed. Rougher surfaces and heavier loads usually mean more friction. Friction is useful, because walking, gripping and braking all depend on it, but it also wears surfaces down and turns useful energy into heat.
English.everyday_example: Your shoes grip the floor because of friction. On a wet, polished floor there is far less grip, so your foot slides.

local_example.text: Bicycle brakes, the grip of sandals on a muddy path during the monsoon, and the wear on a rope all involve friction.
local_example.appropriate_usage: Use as a general local-context draft only until reviewed; do not present it as a claim about any specific place or practice.

common_misconceptions: Friction is always a problem and should always be removed.
Friction acts only once an object is already moving.

observe_around_you.invitation: Find one object and three different surfaces — smooth floor, rough ground, and something in between.
observe_around_you.what_to_do: Give the object the same push on each surface and mark where it stops.
observe_around_you.what_to_notice: Same push, different stopping distance. Now try to push it so gently that it does not move at all, and see how much harder that is to do on the rough surface.
observe_around_you.concept_link: Friction opposes motion and depends on the surfaces in contact. It also explains the thing you just felt: it takes more force to start something moving than to keep it moving.

think_question: Why is it harder to walk on a wet, polished floor than on a dry, rough one?

reasoning_guide.correct_feedback: Good reasoning: you connected the reduced friction to losing grip and slipping.
reasoning_guide.partial_feedback: You are close. Say what happens to the friction on a wet floor, and what that does to your grip.
reasoning_guide.misconception_feedback: Friction is not only a nuisance. Here it is the very thing that lets you walk. What happens when there is less of it?

challenge.question: Give one example where friction helps you and one where friction wastes energy or causes damage.
challenge.hint: Think about how you stop a bicycle, and about why machine parts need oil.
progressive_hints: Think about how you stop a bicycle, and about why machine parts need oil.
Helpful friction lets something grip. Unhelpful friction wears parts out or heats them up.
Write one full sentence for each example, naming the surfaces that rub together.
challenge.solution: Answers differ. A helpful example: brake pads gripping a wheel to stop a bicycle, or shoes gripping the ground. A costly example: friction inside an engine turning fuel energy into heat and wearing the parts down, which is why oil is used.

quiz_questions.question: Friction between two surfaces always acts
options: in the same direction as the motion
only when the surfaces are wet
quiz_questions.explanation: Friction opposes sliding, so it acts opposite to the motion or attempted motion.
quiz_questions.hint: Friction makes things harder to slide, not easier.
progressive_hints: Friction makes things harder to slide, not easier.
If it pushed the same way as the motion, a sliding box would speed up by itself.
